Smart contracts are programs that execute automatically on a blockchain, and their correctness is vital for maintaining the integrity of these systems. This paper introduces HELLMHOLTZ, a static checker designed to verify smart contracts in the Tezos blockchain by leveraging refinement types and an abstract interpreter. HELLMHOLTZ enforces type safety, ensures that assets are only transferred to addresses matching specific regular expressions, verifies that critical functions are exclusively invoked by authorized contracts, and guarantees the absence of runtime exceptions such as division by zero, array out-of-bounds access, and gas overages. HELLMHOLTZ is applicable to contracts written in Michelson, Michelson's predecessor language for the Ligo platform. The tool has been implemented and tested on a suite comprising both functional contracts developed for this study and those selected from the Tezos testnet, demonstrating its practical efficacy.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) have proven to be highly successful in Graph Classification tasks; however, critical questions regarding their underlying mechanics remain largely unanswered. In this study, we introduce a graph convolutional pooling (GCP) framework designed to illuminate GCNs. Our research reveals that graph convolutions function as matched filtering, effectively extracting node embeddings by aligning aggregated features with specific patterns. Furthermore, we establish a novel graph convolutional pooling function that aggregates these embedded representations into definitive class predictions through straightforward mechanisms. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional efficacy of the proposed GCP framework in illuminating GCNs while simultaneously achieving state-of-the-art outcomes across multiple real-world graph datasets.

Using a three-dimensional $f(R)$ gravity theory formulated as a Chern-Simons gauge action involving an $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ group, we derive an action for a minimally coupled massless scalar field. This process establishes a connection between gravity and scalar field theory within Euclidean anti-de Sitter (AdS) asymptotic 3D AdS spacetimes. We demonstrate this validity through two specific cases: first, by showing that the on-shell action variation for a rotating black hole with hair is reciprocal between the gravitational and scalar fields; second, by confirming reciprocity for soliton solutions in the presence of a gauge interaction. Consequently, our work provides a framework to describe rotating black holes with hair and solitons within the context of 3D gravity with a negative cosmological constant and matter interactions.

The concept of reverse symmetry, introduced by H. F. Hofmann and R. Hofmann, involves the formation of pairs where one object is a morphism directed toward another, while the second involves a morphism directed toward the first; this structure within a category exhibits properties akin to group-like behavior. In a broader context, a duality of this concept has been explored through the lens of solid functors, where morphisms flow in the opposite direction (from the second object back to the first), suggesting a group-like interpretation for this structural arrangement. The authors demonstrate that a rigorous definition of a "dual non-reversible symmetry" can be established using a specific membrane concept. They further explore how a duality applies to this result, proposing a concept of "dual membrane" to define it formally. Finally, a geometric representation involving a specific type of bent-membrane structure is introduced to provide a group-like understanding of the dual concept. These membranes have been applied to the study of Witten's $\sigma$-model, yielding insights into the geometric formulation of its supersymmetry generators.

Ultrasound elastography (UE) estimates tissue stiffness by analyzing tissue deformation under ultrasound imaging, serving as a primary method for cancer detection and characterization. A primary obstacle in UE is the assumption of parallel acoustic and mechanical wave propagation, which causes traditional elastography to underestimate lateral displacements. This study introduces Virtual Acquisition, which synthesizes a focused beam by utilizing actual received data from the transmission beam. By integrating Virtual Acquisition with UE, the method achieves more precise lateral displacement measurements. Comparisons with standard UE demonstrate that Virtual-Assisted UE (VAUE) yields superior displacement estimation accuracy, particularly for shear waves propagating perpendicular to the probing direction. The enhanced accuracy of VAUE is especially valuable in clinical settings, where precise stiffness mapping of organs like the liver and breast is required.

This work introduces a prototype system, named Rational, that generates pseudocode from executable algorithm implementations. While existing algorithms-to-text tools often produce output too abstract to connect with implementations or riddled with grammatical issues, our aim is to create a practical aid for both demonstrating and explaining code. To achieve this, we implemented a working version of the system and tested it on 100 algorithm implementations sourced from LeetCode. We also created a user study involving 20 computer science undergraduates, in which participants used Rational to rate the code it generated. The system successfully achieved a 3.5 out of 5 rating for task solvability and a 3.2 out of 5 rating for satisfaction with the text. We describe the system's design, functionality, and evaluation methods, along with plans for future enhancements.

Let $\mathbf{P}$ denote the class of all finite partially ordered sets. For any specific $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbf{P}$, $R(\mathbf{p})$ represents the smallest integer $n$ such that every Boolean algebra of rank $n$ contains a substructure isomorphic to $\mathbf{p}$. In this study, we investigate $R(\mathbf{p})$ when $\mathbf{p}$ forms a "V-shape," defined as having a linear representation $1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5$ where elements $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ constitute two distinct pairs of incomparable elements. By examining $R(\mathbf{p})$ across all such V-shaped configurations, we derive an enhanced upper bound for $R(\mathbf{p})$ for any $\mathbf{p}$ that fits within the broader category of unimodal posets. Furthermore, we determine the exact value of $R(\mathbf{p})$ for the particular case of $\langle 1,2,3,4,5\rangle$. These contributions advance prior work initiated by the authors in reference [6].

We examine the $d$-dimensional $k$-means problem, which involves partitioning $n$ points into $k$ clusters to maximize the minimum diameter of any cluster's diameter. This online variant necessitates maintaining a solution that maximizes this minimum diameter as points arrive sequentially. Prior research established a randomized algorithm achieving an approximation ratio of $\Omega(d^{1/4})$ relative to the optimal offline maximum diameter. In this study, we introduce an efficient data structure that maintains a grouping with a minimum diameter of at least $\frac{1}{1000} \cdot \frac{n}{d^{2}}$ times the optimal offline maximum diameter. Consequently, we achieve an approximation ratio of $f(d) = \frac{1}{1000} \cdot \frac{n}{d^{2}}$ times the optimal offline maximum. Furthermore, our structure requires only $O(n \cdot d^{2})$ operations for updates and queries, storing $O(n \cdot d^{2})$ queries and space complexity of $O(n \cdot d^{2})$.

This research examines a family of stochastic games defined on infinite, discrete, directed graphs where graph nodes represent system configurations subject to stochastic transitions. These graphs are organized into a specific hierarchy, and both players control the system's movement; the drive player aims to guide the system to a target set, while the drift player seeks to prevent it. The system incurs a long-term average cost, making the games' value equal to the optimal long-term average cost the e-bots can achieve. The study focuses on scenarios where the hierarchy permits the e-bots to execute divissions, allowing them to divide the target set into disjoint subsets with divission values representing the minimum long-term average cost to reach each subset individually. It is demonstrated that the divide value serves as an upper bound for the game's value, and under graph expansion conditions, this bound becomes tight, and the e-bots can practically realize the divission strategy to execute the divission.

Deep learning has recently emerged as a prominent technique for denoising low-dose CT images, which are now standard in clinical settings despite containing significant noise. Among these methods, Unsupervised Low-Dose CT Denoising (ULCDD) techniques are particularly valuable because they require no paired training data, thereby eliminating the need for retraining after each new CT scanner installation. CycleGAN represents a notable ULCDD method that utilizes two Cycle-consistent Generative Adversarial Networks (CycleConsistent GANs) to avoid any external reference data. However, previous CycleGAN models suffer from excessive computational costs and poor convergence speeds, issues this study aims to resolve by introducing a new Low-Dose CT Denoising CycleGAN framework. The core innovation lies in the Low-Dose CT Denoising CycleConsistent Transforms (LDCCTs), which employ two independent GANs to learn inverse mappings between low-dose and normal-dose domains via identity mapping and colorization. These LDCCTs are then integrated into CycleGAN through AdaSwitching and Instance Normalization (AdaIN) to enable end-to-end training. The resulting framework, called AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN (ASC-GAN), features a switching mechanism that allows the model to dynamically select between identity and colorization transformations during inference. Extensive experiments confirm that ASC-GAN surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

Pre-training models using vast amounts of unlabeled data has recently yielded significant advancements in various tasks, yet dialogue understanding stands out as a major exception. In this work, we introduce a new pre-training framework for task-oriented dialogue understanding that leverages a large corpus of labeled data specifically suited for tasking. We call this framework SPACE-2 (SPACE Pre-training Enhancement 2). Our framework is built on two key pillars: a new Semi-Automatic Labeling Enhancement (SALE) strategy and a new Label-Aware Contrastive Pre-training (LACP) method. SALE refines existing annotation pipelines by introducing a self-correction mechanism and a multi-stage filtering process, resulting in a high-quality, robust dialogue dataset. Meanwhile, LACP fine-tunes the contrastive pre-training approach by explicitly incorporating label information, allowing the model to better align utterances with their corresponding system actions (such as "no" or "yes"). Together, these innovations allow us to train a high-performing dialogue model that achieves state-of-the-art results on two major dialogue understanding benchmarks, CAMQ and CAMQA, using only a subset of the original training data.

This paper introduces the concept of conformal Ricci-Yamabe solitons applied to the geometric structure of an ideal fluid spacetime while deriving several associated formulas. It further establishes specific conditions under which this novel soliton stabilizes into a trivial soliton and presents a concrete example to validate the theoretical findings.

This study examines the behavior of rotating halo nuclei, focusing on the influence of spin-orbit interactions and angular momentum decoupling. We observe that the characteristic properties of the halo are notably resilient to most distortions in the core, with the notable exception of the strong spin-uncoupling effect. In nuclei exhibiting this specific effect, the coupling between the two components of the core can be significantly altered by rotation. Furthermore, we find that the core's structural integrity may be compromised at specific rotational frequencies, a phenomenon that subsequently impacts the properties of the extending halo.

Dependent largely on optical flow for its success, BasicVSR+ serves as a recurrent architecture designed to handle unconstrained video super-resolution. Nevertheless, it encounters two primary obstacles: the introduction of accumulated misalignments during integration and the compounding of super-resolved errors over time. To address these issues, we introduce BasicVSR++ (also described as BasicVSR++), which enhances video super-resolution for unbounded streams by focusing on two key improvements. Firstly, the method employs a high-frequency feature alignment strategy, aligning high-frequency information adaptively to significantly mitigate misalignment issues. Secondly, it replaces fixed recursive down-sampling with a high-quality feature converter, effectively preventing the recursive amplification of super-resolved errors. Extensive trials on two distinct datasets confirm that BasicVSR++ surpasses both previous and current state-of-the-art benchmarks.

Precise predictions for physics processes at future energy scales require the rigorous calculation of gauge boson radiation, a task complicated by the lack of established, universal methods for estimating $W/Z$ bosons in multi-body final states. This study introduces a novel framework for determining the radiation of weak vector bosons in high-energy muon collisions, leveraging the equivalence theorem to model the interaction of $W/Z$ and photon via a unified set of effective vector bosons. This novel formalism employs radiation kernels featuring logarithmic enhancements to capture non-linear dynamics, thereby facilitating numerical integration to achieve consistent predictions for multi-particle events involving weak bosons. We validate this methodology by analyzing the Higgsstrahlung process ($\mu^{+}\mu^{-} \rightarrow W^{+}W^{-}Z$) and the four-vector-boson scattering ($\mu^{+}\mu^{-} \rightarrow W^{+}W^{-}Z Z$) at a proposed 38 TeV muon collider, demonstrating that the model yields accurate results for both $Z$-pole resonances and off-shell regimes.

This study examines a model-based reinforcement learning framework where agents learn models of their environments to support additional tasks via the addition of new modular components. We demonstrate that when agents restrict themselves to learning only modular parts of their environmental models, it guarantees successful multi-task extension without compromising task-invariant knowledge already applied to the system. In contrast, we provide a counterexample showing that standard approaches, which allow for the unconditional expansion of models by adding new modules, can lead to configurations where task-specific information contaminates shared, task-independent representations. We further introduce an explanatory intuition behind this phenomenon and introduce a formal definition identifying when modular system architectures possess the capability to securely support model-based multi-task reinforcement learning.

Sequential sampling is essential for many statistical applications, particularly when dealing with large target populations where a geographically balanced representation in a sample is critical for effective data analysis. However, existing methods often struggle to balance this balance with statistical efficiency, as they typically yield samples exhibiting higher variability and weaker spatial correlation structures compared to others. This paper introduces a new algorithm designed to geographically balance a sequential sampling process targeting a continuously varying phenomenon. The approach begins by dividing the study area into a grid of cells and initially selects a set of locations based on a standard geographically balanced technique. Subsequently, the method chooses additional sampling points using a spatially myopic criterion that incorporates a spatial smoothing component. This component leverages estimates of the phenomenon in neighboring cells to guide selection, ensuring selected values are spatially distinct while avoiding duplication of already sampled data. Simulation results indicate that this new method successfully delivers spatially balanced realizations with lower variance and higher spatial dissimilarity, all while maintaining efficiency comparable to a simple random sample of the same size.

We introduce a learning-based technique to correct extrinsic parameters for eye-in-hand cameras using only a single image. Although the method was developed for a single degree of freedom (1-DoF) calibration, it can be extended to more complex systems, including those with multiple degrees of freedom. By leveraging recent advancements in neural networks, this approach requires only minimal manual intervention, such as identifying a feature in 3D space and its corresponding projection in the image plane. Specifically, the user marks a cylindrical axis in the scene and identifies its silhouette in the image. The neural component then estimates the current extrinsic parameters by aligning a rendered model of the cylinder axis with the observed feature in the scene. The three-dimensional position of the axis is known beforehand, and the user can easily locate it. The system described is flexible, allowing the addition of new axes or cylinders as long as their 3D coordinates are accessible. The neural aspect of the technique is inherently extensible for incorporating multiple feature sets. The primary advantage of this system is the ability to adjust extrinsic parameters dynamically and in real time, a significant challenge in the current state of robotics. The method was evaluated on an industrial robotic arm equipped with a KUKA YUKO camera, demonstrating measurement accuracy within approximately 1 millimeter.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) have demonstrated significant potential in numerous domains, prompting this study's investigation into utilizing them to conditionally sample from the probability distribution of an inverse problem after regularisation. We establish that using L2 regularization within a well-posed forward problem allows CGANs to learn an mapping that conditions noisy realizations of the basic forward problem on low-risk regularised solutions of that problem. We further demonstrate the applicability of this approach to ill-posed and operator equations, where it serves to conditionally sample from the set of solutions that match specified target data values. Lastly, we highlight the framework's versatility by addressing the conditional ill-posed deconvolution problem, showcasing the generation of diverse solutions that reverse a convolution process while matching particular data criteria.

Invariant surfaces function as powerful tools for analyzing the behavior of dynamical systems, yet extending their use to fractional systems faces challenges due to the lack of standard transformation methods. This article explores the conditions required for fractional difference coefficient systems to possess two-dimensional invariant subspaces. It further examines how the dynamics on such surfaces mirror those of their corresponding integer-order counterparts. As a practical outcome, this approach is utilized to examine a specific fractional difference coefficient system, confirming that it fails to support an invariant surface.

Terahertz (THz) communications are recognized as promising pathways for future 6G mobile networks, offering vast bandwidths that support extreme data transmission rates. However, deploying THz signals over multi-hop routes presents significant hurdles, primarily due to extensive hardware hardware requirements and difficulties in maintaining stable signal integrity. A critical obstacle in this domain is the necessity for rapid and efficient beam training to identify optimal communication links. This study proposes leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance beam training protocols specifically for THz systems operating across multi-hop environments. In this framework, learning agents autonomously acquire the optimal sequence of beams by interacting with the surrounding state space. The research introduces two distinct RL methodologies: a basic approach that trains a single universal policy to determine beams for all hops independently, and an advanced multi-agent hierarchical structure designed to learn individualized beam configurations for each segment of the link. Comprehensive simulations demonstrate that these suggested methods surpass traditional benchmark techniques by substantially improving end-to-end throughput, total transmission rate, and overall system efficiency.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an advanced, pitch-aware, autoregressive model designed for speech synthesis. While WaveNet has established itself as a state-of-the-art choice for speech generation, previous iterations lacked specific architectural features necessary for precise control over pitch and duration. To address this limitation, QPNet integrates several key innovations: a dilated convolution architecture utilizing quasi-periodic activation functions, explicit duration modeling, and a specialized sampling strategy. These components enable QPNet to produce high-fidelity natural speech with superior efficiency. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses prior pitch-sensitive autoregressive models in both fundamental frequency ($f_0$) accuracy and overall synthesis quality. Furthermore, the model exhibits exceptional scalability; it successfully generates long-duration utterances by leveraging a probabilistic probabilistic approach, a capability where WaveNet often encounters challenges.

Arabic morphology is highly intricate, characterized by a root-and-pattern system along with affixation, which necessitates specialized tools for computational processing and the development of Natural Language Applications (NLP). While the Joint Morphological Analyzer (JAMA) was introduced to address this complexity, the absence of an associated web platform limits its utility for the wider community. To bridge this gap, we created MADARi, a JAMA-based platform designed to deliver morphological analysis, visualize the decomposition into stems and affixes, display the internal structure of trigrams, and facilitate the export of annotated files in both XML and JSON formats. Furthermore, the system supports user registration, allowing academics and practitioners to register, log in, and save their projects. We also implemented a feature enabling users to submit corrections to JAMA's output; these suggestions are stored and will be incorporated into future updates of the analyzer.

Ultraviolet radiation from the host star drives the complex photochemistry of temperate exoplanets, profoundly affecting their atmospheric composition and surface conditions. While UV spectroscopy serves as a primary method for analyzing the atmospheres of transiting planets, current models often neglect photochemical processes, potentially obscuring the true nature of planetary atmospheres. This study investigates the impact of photochemistry on planetary transmission spectra by comparing spectra generated from chemically static models against those produced via a one-dimensional photochemical framework. Our simulations indicate that for planets orbiting Sun-like stars, atmospheric signatures in the visible and near-infrared wavelengths are significantly altered by photochemistry, whereas planets orbiting Main Sequence stars with spectral types earlier than F exhibit minimal deviations. Furthermore, this chemically induced spectral alteration is contingent upon the planetary equilibrium temperature, atmospheric circulation patterns, and the initial elemental inventory of the atmosphere.

Magnetic atom chains embedded in superconductors are a leading candidate for realizing a topological superconducting phase and a zero-energy Majorana bound state (MBS), which could serve as a robust qubit for fault-tolerant quantum computing. A primary method for detecting MBS involves measuring the differential conductance via tunneling spectroscopy; however, this must be done with extreme caution, as other phenomena can produce spurious peaks at zero bias that mimic the signature of MBS. Consequently, distinguishing the true MBS from these mimics is essential. In this work, we propose utilizing the damping of a tunneling probe placed at the ends of a magnetic atom chain in contact with an s-wave superconducting reservoir. We demonstrate that this setup allows for the clear identification of MBS, even in the presence of noise sources such as a quantum critical antiferromagnet. Furthermore, we show that this technique is robust against various forms of magnetic flux, further supporting its viability for experimental realization.

The swift advancement of mobile computing, artificial intelligence, and deep learning has enabled the creation of versatile, user-centric smart devices designed to tackle complex societal challenges. Atlas Road Management System (Atlas Road Management System) is such an innovative platform, built upon the convergence of these cutting-edge technologies to deliver mobile-computing-driven problem solving. Specifically developed as a practical case study, RoadAtlas addresses the detection of pavement anomalies using practical, hands-on methodologies grounded in industry needs.

To realize this goal, RoadAtlas leverages extensive image and defect datasets collected from U.S. highways, utilizing the massive open online course (RoadAtlas) framework. The system operates in a modular design, allowing users to inspect code and data repositories freely via its GitHub repository. Technically, the project employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for the classification of road anomalies, integrating a user-friendly interface and a robust backend infrastructure. By combining these components, RoadAtlas enables the automatic categorization of various types of highway anomalies from image inputs, thereby streamlining the management and inspection of highway infrastructure.

We introduce the concept of a biblactic track and establish a new result demonstrating that shadows adhering to a hyperversorized equivalency condition become biblactic tracks; this general framework subsumes a well-known theorem which states that bi-regularized homomorphic tracks are biblactic tracks.

We introduce a novel approach to the challenge of super-resolution localization of acoustic emissions. This method employs a convolutional neural network trained on a substantial dataset comprising 60,000+ sound samples, each annotated with its precise sound-emitting source location. Our results indicate that this system achieves a mean absolute error of 3.8 cm in horizontal accuracy and 5 cm vertically; notably, when augmented with camera footage for viewpoint context, these figures improve to mean absolute errors of 1.5 cm horizontally and 2 cm vertically. Furthermore, this system has been successfully integrated into a mobile application, making it accessible for broader use.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) function as a potent framework for handling graph-structured data, yet they typically disregard the intrinsic structural details of individual graphs. This shortcoming is particularly problematic for temporal graphs, where incorporating evolution is essential for high performance. To address these issues, we introduce Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (LoGNN), a novel method designed to analyze data on "Lorentzian graphs." These graphs consist of nodes with attributes and directed edges characterized by both specific types and temporal latency. We outline the theoretical underpinnings of our approach, demonstrating its capacity to effectively integrate multi-granularity neighborhood aggregation across various temporal scopes while preserving the precise layout of nodes. Rigorous experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques for link prediction in temporal graphs. Our codebase can be accessed at https://github.com/lo-gnn/LoGNN.

We address the general engagement between a structure and a fluid as a forward variational inequality involving the simultaneous determination of structural boundary movements and stress concentrations. Subsequently, we analyze a class of inverse problems aimed at identifying these interactions. Specifically, we apply Carleman estimates to the associated ill-posed problem to guarantee the unique existence of engagements and the well-posed nature of the problem. Finally, under the assumption of a unique solution, the Hukuhara-Katev approach is utilized to demonstrate the existence of solutions for the inverse problem of engagement.

This work examines the generation of photon number states (Fock states) using long-lived mechanical oscillators coupled with photons via radiation pressure. The study focuses on a single-mode cavity where nonlinear interactions are mediated by a two-level system in a specific superposition of energy levels, enabling a hybrid system to achieve both state-dependent reflection and position-dependent transmission. These dual conditional nonlinearities facilitate optical compression transfer, which, combined with a Markovian environment and a red-detuned single photon, facilitates optomachanical squeezing of a longer-lived mechanical mode. The protocol is validated through a comparison of a three-level system implementation, demonstrating that a simple two-level setup with tailored superposition can produce a highly similar result.

This paper introduces a novel variant of basic modal $\mu$-calculus termed "modal $i$-calculus," which formalizes reasoning about systems involving discrete moving particles. We establish the completeness of its basic fragment and demonstrate that this system is equivalent in expressive power to Basic Stratified Action $\mu$-calculus. The composition of planetesimals that formed in the inner solar system is crucial for understanding planetary evolution. Evidence from the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites indicates their building blocks were predominantly wet, yet existing theories based on inner solar system temperature profiles struggle to explain this moisture. Our findings reveal that form factor equations emerge which are consistent with previously suggested hypotheses by Gromov and Kazakov regarding the form factors of the XXX chain for spins ranging from 1 to $M$. Furthermore, within the context of higher-spin XXZ chains, we establish a connection between the form factors and the quantum $R$-matrix elements found inside the algebraic Bethe Ansatz framework. Finally, based on these results, we propose an infinite set of quantum operators that exhibit mutual scattering phases identical to those of the quantum-R matrix eigenvalue Baxter $T$-equation.

Voice translation (VTC) converts spoken language from one tongue into another, playing a vital role in global communication. State-of-the-art neural models for VTC rely heavily on extensive parallel corpora covering all supported language pairs, a requirement that significantly hampers support for low-resource languages. To circumvent this limitation, we introduce Zero-shot Voice Translation (Z-VTC), enabling synthetic speech conversion for pairs lacking available audio-parallel data. Our method integrates two core elements: an unsupervised alignment module that extracts synchronized features from monolingual sources without needing annotation, followed by a neural architecture that synthesizes spoken audio using these extracted features to achieve VTC capability. We evaluated our system across eight languages using the LibriSpeech corpus, employing Wav2Vec 2.0 for speech extraction and evaluating results using the Mozilla Common Voice dataset. Our approach was tested on eight language pairs with abundant data for single-source languages but sparse or absent for parallel sets. Compared to a strong baseline, our system improves performance by 1.5 to 2.5 Mozilla TCTO (TCTO) scores, with the largest relative gains observed in low-resource scenarios. We have released our codebase publicly at https://github.com/your-org/Z-VTC.

This work presents a novel, rigorous multipolar decomposition applicable to scattering and scattering-related processes, valid throughout the full frequency range. At optical and infrared frequencies, where dipolar and higher-order terms dominate, our method offers a practical means to quantitatively separate and isolate these terms. We demonstrate that this new decomposition yields results consistent with traditional approaches within their shared domains of validity. Furthermore, it enables a precise analysis at longer wavelengths—specifically in the near-infrared range—regarding the individual roles played by multipoles in scattering, scattering-associated measurements, and thermal emission. Building on this framework, we investigate the limitations underlying approximations that decouple optical scattering from optical tuning, and we utilize the decomposition to examine how multipoles contribute to optical losses and the subsequent dissipation of electromagnetic energy. Finally, we apply this formalism to analyze and predict the effects of breaking the long-wavelength approximation within plasmonic nanostructures and metamaterials, and we explore its implications for understanding and optimizing near-field optical influence computations and scattering.

"Orbital ordering in magnetic compounds of transition metals arises from the selective mixing of metal d orbitals with itinerant electron states, while non-bonding t2g states prevent simultaneous mixing with all e-g orbitals. This paper examines the distinct characteristics of such selective blending in oxides containing K2Cr2O3 structure types, focusing on the contrasting behaviors of 4d and 5d electron systems. Our findings reveal that while 4d e-g electrons remain largely localized, 5d e-g electrons in Ru2O3 and Fe2O3 mix significantly with itinerant t2g electrons, resulting in a contraction of the band gap upon removal of orbital ordering in 5d compounds."

This work introduces the notion of relative quantum cohomology for Laurent loop Laurentianization, specifically within the context of torus action. We demonstrate that quantum deformation of the (relative) Cherkis bowdend relation is satisfied by the Laurentianization process associated with torus actions on an algebraic variety. Additionally, we introduce the concept of Laurentianization in Witten's disk invariants, specifically examining the relative case, suggesting its capacity to facilitate the derivation of relative three-point disk invariants following such modifications.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have significantly advanced the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases, they frequently encounter challenges with generalization when applied to new datasets. A primary cause for this limitation is the lack of transferable patient-specific information across different datasets. This paper introduces a solution to enhance model generalization by integrating patient-aware image modification directly into the pre-training phase. We utilize Chest X-Ray (CXR) ray datasets to demonstrate that initial training with these adapted images significantly improves performance on a target dataset for disease detection tasks. Specifically, we evaluate two leading pulmonary disease detectors on the CheXpert dataset following training on the MIMIC-CXR dataset using these modified approaches. The results indicate superior detector performance when the proposed methods are applied to the MIMIC-CXR dataset during pre-training compared to standard training protocols.

Increasing reliance on computers for processing and analyzing real-world data has led to a surge in datasets characterized by high dimensionality, large volume, diverse types, and complex relationships. Effectively presenting such multidimensional data remains a significant challenge in the field of information visualization. Existing tools often fall short, failing to offer an optimal balance of intuitive design, user-friendly interaction, and comprehensive data display. To address this gap, we developed ViDaExpert, a desktop application built on the Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) framework within Microsoft Excel. Excel was selected due to its ubiquitous nature and native capabilities for storing and managing extensive datasets. By leveraging Excel's robust features, ViDaExpert enables the simultaneous visualization of data points, dimensions, and values through various view modes, including parallel coordinates, scatter plots, and heatmaps. It incorporates advanced functionalities such as data aggregation, multiple filtering strategies, and the generation of diverse statistical summaries. Furthermore, the tool supports the visualization of derived data through various line charts, bar graphs, and pie charts. Our evaluation demonstrates that this new interface is effective for representing multidimensional data sets, proving particularly valuable for experts in domains involving extensive datasets.

This study introduces a new metric for evaluating the accuracy of numerical approximations for Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives and integrals, formulated within a specific domain and evaluated on external regions. This approach determines the true values by applying domain deformation techniques combined with direct evaluation of the Cauchy data integral, enabling its application to both integer- and non-integer-order Newtonian potentials. The authors demonstrate the method's efficacy through several representative cases, highlighting its particular advantage in providing precise true values for Riemann-Liouville derivatives and integrals outside the computation domain—a critical requirement for implementing domain boundary conditions in time-fractional partial differential equations solved numerically.
